supplementary_news.content_title: Updated Flu Covid And RSV Vaccines Roll Out Nationwide
supplementary_news.content: As the leaves start to turn and autumn settles in, a familiar but serious concern is again at the forefront for communities across North America: the arrival of respiratory virus season. This fall, the convergence of influenza, Covid-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) has prompted health officials and medical organizations in both the United States and Canada to roll out updated vaccination campaigns, offering new guidance in the face of evolving viral threats and shifting federal oversight. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and corroborated by CNN and Mezha , seasonal influenza activity is currently low at the national level. However, certain regions, particularly Washington state's King County, have seen a noticeable uptick in emergency department visits for flu since mid-August 2026. The CDC has responded by posting guidance online that largely follows last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19 vaccines. This comes as the agency navigates changes to its vaccine advisory committee and ongoing legal challenges, which have complicated the release of new, unified federal vaccine guidance. Amid this uncertainty, independent reviews of the 2026-27 vaccine formulations were published in September in the journal JAMA . These reviews, led by the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project, have informed updated recommendations from a coalition of medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, emphasized the ongoing necessity for clear, evidence-based guidance. “Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said at a news briefing, as reported by CNN . He added, “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.” For Americans and Canadians alike, access to vaccines is robust this year. Flu, Covid-19, and RSV immunizations are available at most major pharmacies, and, reassuringly, insurers have indicated that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations. Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, noted, “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives.” She stressed that the 2026-27 recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence and shaped by what physicians are seeing in their practices. North of the border, the government of New Brunswick has launched a province-wide respiratory illness prevention campaign, announcing that updated influenza and Covid-19 vaccines will be available for free to everyone aged six months and older starting October 13, 2026. As reported by the Fredericton Independent , Dr. Yves Léger, New Brunswick’s chief medical officer of health, stated, “If you are eligible for both, we encourage you to get them at the same visit.” He highlighted that these vaccines reduce the chance of serious illness, hospitalization, and community spread. Appointments can be scheduled through the government’s website or by contacting participating community pharmacies, and select primary care providers will also have doses available. Special attention is being paid to high-risk groups, including those aged 65 and older, residents of long-term care facilities, individuals with chronic health conditions, and pregnant women. For children who are averse to injections, the province is offering FluMist, a nasal spray influenza vaccine, for those aged two to seventeen. Families are encouraged to check eligibility and book appointments through their healthcare providers or local public health offices. So, who should get which vaccine, and when? The updated guidance is clear but nuanced. For RSV, recommendations cover several groups. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics and echoed by Mezha , older adults—specifically people aged 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75—should receive one dose. This is not an annual shot; one dose should protect recipients for the entire season. Pregnant individuals are advised to get the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, between September 1 and March 1, reflecting a shift in timing due to a later and more severe RSV season. Infants younger than eight months should receive an RSV monoclonal antibody unless their mother was vaccinated during pregnancy. Children between eight and nineteen months who are at high risk should also receive the monoclonal antibody, and immunosuppressed adults are likewise advised to get a single dose. For flu, the message is straightforward: everyone six months and older should get an annual flu shot. Adults 65 and older are encouraged to opt for an enhanced vaccine—high-dose, adjuvanted, or recombinant—when available, but should not delay vaccination if these are not in stock. Notably, for the first time in 2026, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for adults 50 and older. Pregnant people are recommended to receive the inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccine, not the nasal spray, as per the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Dr. Christina Davidson of ACOG explained, “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people.” She also noted the added benefit that vaccination during pregnancy can confer immunity to the newborn. October is widely regarded as the optimal time to get the flu shot, ensuring protection throughout the peak of the season. Providers use the catchy slogan “flu before boo” to remind patients to get vaccinated before Halloween. The updated Covid-19 vaccines are recommended for adults, especially those over 19, and particularly for people 65 and older, who should receive a second dose six months after the initial one to maintain protection. Infants between six and twenty-three months, children in high-risk groups, and immunocompromised individuals aged six months and older are also prioritized. Pregnant and breastfeeding people are strongly advised to get the Covid-19 vaccine as well. Dr. Davidson stressed, “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses. I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth or birth defects.” For those who have recently recovered from Covid-19, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the updated vaccine. As Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer of the American Medical Association put it, “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event—if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together—think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.” In both the U.S. and Canada, vaccines are available at most major pharmacies, covered by insurance, and, for children, accessible through federal programs like Vaccines for Children. Information and booking resources are readily available on government websites, making it as easy as possible for families to get protected. This fall, as the air grows crisp and routines shift, public health experts are urging everyone to take advantage of these updated vaccines. With a clear roadmap from medical organizations and support from local governments, communities have the tools to stay healthy and keep respiratory viruses at bay. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Business Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio doctor group backs childhood vaccines amid political split Samantha Hendrickson Columbus Dispatch Oct. 5, 2026, 5:03 a.m. ET The Ohio State Medical Association is reaffirming its support for traditional vaccine schedules from the American Academy of Pediatrics. This comes amid rising vaccine skepticism and record measles cases in both the United States and Ohio. The association's political arm recently endorsed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has expressed vaccine hesitancy. The Ohio State Medical Association is sticking to traditional vaccine recommendations following their political arm's endorsement of a more vaccine-hesitant gubernatorial candidate and ongoing clash between federal health officials and the nation's top pediatric organization. The Ohio State Medical Association (OSMA), which describes itself as the leading voice for physicians, residents and medical students in Ohio, announced its support for the American Academy of Pediatrics' (AAP) child and adolescent vaccine schedule on Sept. 29. Once a set of golden rules in medicine, AAP's vaccine recommendations, which include doses from birth to age 17 that protect against 18 diseases, have come under more scrutiny as vaccine skepticism rises in the United States. As such skepticism has grown, so have the number of cases of diseases that have long been preventable with vaccines. There are currently over 3,600 cases of measles in the United States, the highest number since 1991. Ohio has reported 196 measles cases – double its case count for 2025. This skepticism has wound itself tightly in the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), led by known vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Under Kennedy, who has no formal medical training, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rolled back or downgraded several vaccine recommendations such hepatitis A and B, rotavirus, flu, meningococcal disease and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) for all people groups. The HHS bypassed its standard process of consulting the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) during a public meeting. Earlier this year, AAP and other health organizations sued the federal government over the roll backs. A judge granted a stay on the CDC's changes and reverted to July 2025 vaccine recommendations. Dr. Gary Katz, OSMA's president and an emergency physician, told The Dispatch that one of the "key advancements" in public health has been through prevention of infectious diseases, and vaccines are vital and scientifically sound prevention tools. But he also acknowledged that doctors and patients alike are in a new age of sourcing information, and that requires deeper conversations between those doctors and patients to dispel incomplete or "outright wrong" information. "It's understandable to have questions..." Katz said. "I encourage them to have those conversations about what they've heard, why they might be afraid or might be hesitant to follow what's been so well established as good public health policy and recommendations, and have those conversations with their families." Political arm decision splits Ohio doctors In September, the OSMA's political arm endorsed Republican tech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio governor's race over Democratic Dr. Amy Acton, who previously directed the Ohio Department of Health during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ramaswamy has publicly expressed regret over receiving the COVID-19 vaccine, as well as opposed mask and vaccine mandates. His wife, Dr. Apoorva Ramaswamy, a physician and assistant professor at Ohio State University, received the vaccine. OSMA's political arm, which Katz said is not the same as the organization itself and not representative of all members of the organization, endorsed Ramaswamy after meeting with Dr. Ramaswamy. OSMA PAC Chair Dr. Anne Taylor said that Ramaswamy's commitment to reducing administrative burdens and insurance barriers on doctors as one of the reasons they chose to support him. Some physicians signed an open letter, starting: "When a medical organization backs a candidate who threatens the very foundation of patient care, it betrays the core duty of our profession."
